name: Nominatim
purpose: Geocoding and reverse-geocoding engine over OpenStreetMap data, resolving place names and addresses to coordinates and vice versa, self-hostable or used via the OSM-operated public service.
journalism_use_case: Batch-geocode a leaked or scraped dataset of addresses — property registers, company filings, aid-delivery records — so it can be mapped and spatially joined. Reverse geocoding also turns coordinates in image metadata or ADS-B records into readable place names for a story.
pros: Self-hostable, which is the decisive property for batch geocoding: a dataset of addresses sent to a commercial geocoder discloses your entire investigation to that vendor
GPL-3.0 with active maintenance (v5.3.3, 2026-10-14) and a documented import process, so a regional instance is a realistic project
Reverse geocoding is as well supported as forward, which matters for turning coordinates into publishable place descriptions
No API key or quota when self-hosted, so batch work over hundreds of thousands of records is practical
cons: Self-hosting is a real undertaking: a planet import needs terabyte-class disk and many hours; a regional extract is far more manageable but still a day's work
The OSM public instance has a strict usage policy that forbids heavy batch use, so the convenient path is explicitly not available for the main use case

Geocoding accuracy depends on OSM address coverage, which is excellent in some countries and poor in others — and silent mismatches (a street name matched in the wrong city) are the dangerous failure mode
102 open issues and operational complexity around index tuning and updates
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 4,571 stars with 102 open issues, release v5.3.3 (2026-10-14), pushed 2026-11-16, GPL-3.0. The OSM Foundation's usage policy for the public instance (which restricts bulk geocoding) is documented by the project and is the key operational constraint.
assessment: Self-host a regional instance if geocoding is a recurring need — the privacy and quota arguments both point the same way, and a country-level extract is affordable. For your profile the essential quality control is to validate a sample of geocoded results manually and to record match confidence, because a dataset where 8% of addresses resolved to the wrong city will produce a map that looks right and is wrong.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v5.3.3 (2026-10-14), 4,571 stars, 102 open issues. Regular releases on a 5.x line under OSM-adjacent institutional maintenance.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on the engine. ODbL applies to the data: publishing a geocoded derived database triggers attribution and share-alike obligations. The OSM public instance's usage policy additionally restricts bulk use — a service term, not a licence term.
costs: No fee. Self-hosting estimate: a country-sized extract needs roughly tens to low hundreds of GB of disk and a few hours of import on a modest VM; a full planet instance needs terabyte-class storage and substantially more. Assumptions: PostgreSQL/PostGIS backend, regional extract.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps the addresses you geocode entirely private — the main reason to do it, since batch-geocoding an investigation's address list through a commercial API hands over the target list. The public OSM instance sees queries and disallows bulk use.
alternatives: Photon (komoot) for a faster, more typo-tolerant self-hosted geocoder
Pelias for a modular geocoder combining multiple data sources
Commercial geocoding APIs only for non-sensitive data, accepting the disclosure
blockers: Public instance forbids bulk geocoding; self-hosting required for the primary use case
summary: Geocoding and reverse-geocoding engine over OpenStreetMap data, resolving place names and addresses to coordinates and vice…

name: Photon (komoot geocoder)
purpose: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch-based geocoder over OpenStreetMap data, designed for fast typo-tolerant search-as-you-type and reverse geocoding, with prebuilt import dumps available.
journalism_use_case: Fast, typo-tolerant geocoding of messy address data — the common case with leaked registries, handwritten records and OCR output where addresses are misspelled, abbreviated or partially transcribed and a strict geocoder returns nothing.
pros: Typo tolerance is the practical differentiator over Nominatim for investigative data, which is almost always dirty — an OCR'd address with two character errors still resolves
Prebuilt import dumps mean you can stand up an instance without running the OSM import yourself, which removes the main operational barrier
Apache-2.0 (more permissive than Nominatim's GPL-3.0) with active maintenance (1.3.0, 2026-08-07; pushed 2026-11-15)
Self-hosted, so batch geocoding of sensitive address lists stays internal
cons: Requires Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, adding a stateful service to operate alongside whatever else you run
Typo tolerance cuts both ways: a fuzzy match to the wrong place looks like a successful geocode, so confidence thresholds and manual validation matter more here than with a strict geocoder
Address coverage is still bounded by OSM, so countries with thin address data remain difficult regardless of matching quality
Not distinguished from the unrelated s0md3v/Photon crawler in search results, which causes genuine confusion when researching it; 41 open issues
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,197 stars with 41 open issues, release 1.3.0 (2026-08-07), pushed 2026-11-15, Apache-2.0. The public photon.komoot.io instance exists for light use; komoot operates it as a courtesy, so heavy batch use should be self-hosted.
assessment: My preferred self-hosted geocoder for investigative data specifically because the input is usually dirty — and the prebuilt dumps make it the faster of the two to deploy. For your profile pair it with a validation step: record the match score for every geocoded row, review everything below a threshold manually, and never map a dataset without reporting the proportion that failed or matched weakly. That reporting discipline is what makes a geocoded map defensible.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-15, latest release 1.3.0 (2026-08-07), 3,197 stars, 41 open issues. Regular releases under corporate maintenance (komoot) with a clean tracker.
model_or_data_licence: OpenStreetMap data is ODbL 1.0; prebuilt import dumps are derived OSM data and carry the same obligations.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. ODbL applies to the data and to derived databases you publish.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a JVM service plus an Elasticsearch/OpenSearch node — one moderate VM for a country-scale index. Prebuilt dumps save the import compute. Assumptions: regional index, self-hosted.
privacy: Self-hosted geocoding keeps your address lists internal. The public komoot instance sees whatever you send it — avoid for investigative data.
alternatives: Nominatim for strict matching and the reference OSM geocoder
Pelias where you need to blend OSM with other address sources
libpostal for address parsing and normalisation before geocoding
summary: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch-based geocoder over OpenStreetMap data, designed for fast typo-tolerant search-as-you-type and reverse…

name: Pelias
purpose: Modular open-source geocoder that blends multiple data sources — OpenStreetMap, OpenAddresses, Who's on First, geonames — behind a single API, with autocomplete and structured query support.
journalism_use_case: Geocoding where OSM alone is insufficient: blending OpenAddresses and other sources gives materially better address coverage in several countries, which matters when your dataset is national property or company registrations and Nominatim's coverage has gaps.
pros: Multi-source blending is the architectural advantage: OpenAddresses in particular fills address gaps that OSM leaves, improving match rates on national registry data
Structured query support (separate fields for street, city, postcode) materially improves accuracy over free-text geocoding of registry data
MIT licensed with a modular design, so you can import only the sources relevant to your region
Still maintained (v7.11.0, 2026-09-25; pushed 2026-10-21) after the original sponsor (Mapzen) wound down — a community continuation that survived
cons: Multi-service architecture (api, placeholder, pip, libpostal, Elasticsearch, importers) is the heaviest geocoding deployment of the three here — meaningfully more operational work than Photon
Small community for the api repository (259 stars) with 137 open issues, and documentation is spread across many repositories, making orientation slow
Blending sources introduces its own ambiguity: the same place can appear from several sources with different geometries, and deduplication quality varies
Original corporate sponsor is gone, so long-term direction depends on a modest community — a continuity consideration for infrastructure you would run for years
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 259 stars with 137 open issues, release v7.11.0 (2026-09-25), pushed 2026-10-21, MIT licence. The project survived the shutdown of its original sponsor (Mapzen), which is itself evidence of community commitment, though the contributor base is modest.
assessment: Choose it only when coverage genuinely requires multi-source blending — for example national address work in a country where OpenAddresses is strong and OSM is weak. Otherwise Photon is substantially less work for comparable results on dirty data. For your profile I would test match rates for your specific country on both before committing, since that empirical answer, not the architecture, determines which is right.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-21, latest release v7.11.0 (2026-09-25), 259 stars, 137 open issues. Recent release and commits, but a modest contributor base post-Mapzen and a substantial backlog across a multi-repository project. Stable rather than actively developed.
model_or_data_licence: Mixed by source: OpenStreetMap is ODbL 1.0; OpenAddresses sources carry a range of per-source licences, some with attribution or redistribution conditions; Who's on First is CC-BY. These differ and must be checked per region you import.
licence_restrictions: Code is MIT. The data licensing is genuinely mixed and is the item needing attention: an OpenAddresses import can include sources whose terms restrict redistribution, so publishing a derived dataset requires per-source review.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: several services plus Elasticsearch — realistically two or more VMs for a country-scale deployment, more operational attention than Photon. Assumptions: self-hosted, regional imports.
privacy: Self-hosted, so geocoding stays internal. Public demo instances see your queries.
alternatives: Photon for a lighter self-hosted geocoder with good typo tolerance
Nominatim as the OSM reference implementation
libpostal alone for address parsing if your bottleneck is normalisation rather than lookup
blockers: Mixed data-source licensing requires per-source review before publishing derived datasets
summary: Modular open-source geocoder that blends multiple data sources — OpenStreetMap, OpenAddresses, Who's on First, geonames…

name: mapillary_tools
purpose: Command-line tools for processing and uploading street-level imagery to Mapillary, including geotagging from GPS tracks, sequence organisation and metadata handling.
journalism_use_case: Two uses: processing your own ground-truth imagery (a reporter driving a route with a dashcam) into a geotagged sequence for later reference, and understanding the metadata structure of Mapillary imagery you use for geolocation verification against a photograph.
pros: Mapillary's crowd-sourced street-level imagery is often the only street-view coverage available in countries Google does not photograph — which is precisely where much conflict and corruption reporting happens
Geotagging from GPS tracks lets a reporter turn a drive-through into a reusable, dated visual record of a location, useful when you cannot return
BSD-2-Clause and actively maintained (v0.15.0, 2026-11-04; pushed 2026-11-16) with a clean tracker
Processing happens locally, so you control what is uploaded and when
cons: Uploading contributes your imagery to a Meta-operated platform under its terms — a deliberate disclosure that also reveals where your reporter has been, with timestamps
The tool is for contributing imagery, not for downloading it, so for geolocation verification you need the Mapillary API or streetlevel instead — a distinction that wastes people's time
Narrow scope and engineer-facing; a reporter will not use it directly
Coverage of the platform itself is uneven and contributor-dependent, so the imagery you want may simply not exist
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 320 stars with 33 open issues, release v0.15.0 (2026-11-04), pushed 2026-11-16, BSD-2-Clause. Mapillary's role as a street-level imagery source in regions without commercial coverage is well established in open-source investigation practice.
assessment: Relevant mainly if your team does field work and wants to build a reusable visual record — in which case it is the right tool, with one serious caveat: uploading a geotagged sequence publishes where your reporter drove and when, which can endanger them or their sources in a hostile environment. Process locally, review carefully, and treat the upload decision as an editorial and security judgement rather than a technical step. For consuming imagery for geolocation, use streetlevel or the Mapillary API instead.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v0.15.0 (2026-11-04), 320 stars, 33 open issues. Regular releases under corporate maintenance.
model_or_data_licence: Imagery uploaded to Mapillary is licensed under the platform's terms (historically CC-BY-SA for the imagery database); imagery you consume from Mapillary carries those terms.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. The imagery licensing is the substantive point: check Mapillary's current terms before republishing imagery from the platform in a story, and understand what rights you grant when uploading.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute; bandwidth for uploads. A Mapillary account is required to upload.
privacy: Processing is local; uploading publishes geotagged imagery to a Meta-operated platform, disclosing locations and timestamps of your field movements. This is the dominant consideration for hostile-environment work.
alternatives: streetlevel for downloading panoramas and metadata from Street View, Look Around and Mapillary for verification
The Mapillary API directly for programmatic imagery access
Keeping field imagery entirely internal with your own geotagging scripts (ExifTool can write GPS tags)
blockers: Uploading discloses reporter movements with timestamps to a third-party platform
summary: Command-line tools for processing and uploading street-level imagery to Mapillary, including geotagging from GPS tracks…

name: streetlevel
purpose: Python library for downloading panoramas and metadata from several street-level imagery services, including Google Street View, Apple Look Around, Yandex Panorama and Mapillary, via their internal or public interfaces.
journalism_use_case: The practical workhorse of photograph geolocation: pull panoramas for a candidate location and compare building façades, signage and street furniture against the image you are trying to place — and pull the capture dates, which tell you whether a feature visible in your photo existed when the panorama was taken.
pros: Multi-provider coverage including Apple Look Around and Yandex Panorama is the key advantage: Yandex coverage of Russia, Central Asia and parts of the Middle East is far better than Google's, which matters enormously for reporting on those regions
Programmatic panorama download enables systematic comparison across many candidate locations, which manual Street View browsing cannot
Capture-date metadata is exposed, which is essential for temporal reasoning about what a photograph shows
MIT licensed, actively maintained (v0.13.0 on 2026-11-12, same-day push) with a very clean tracker (5 open issues)
cons: Works against providers' internal or undocumented interfaces, which may breach their terms of service and can break without notice — a legal and reliability consideration you must take knowingly

Requests go directly to the imagery providers, so Google, Apple or Yandex see which locations you are examining — and for Yandex in particular, that disclosure may reach a jurisdiction you are investigating
Small project (249 stars) with a single maintainer, so continuity depends on one person against several moving upstream targets
No licence clarity on the imagery itself: panoramas remain the providers' copyrighted content, so republishing them in a story is a separate rights question
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 249 stars with 5 open issues, release v0.13.0 on 2026-11-12 with same-day push, MIT licence. The reliance on providers' internal interfaces is inherent to the approach and is the acknowledged fragility.
assessment: Genuinely valuable for geolocation in regions where Google coverage is absent, and the Yandex access in particular has no real substitute. For your profile three cautions apply together: route requests through an egress not identifiable as your newsroom, be aware that querying Yandex discloses your interest to a Russian service, and treat panorama images as third-party copyrighted material requiring a rights decision before publication. Expect breakage and keep manual browsing as a fallback.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-12, latest release v0.13.0 published the same day, 249 stars, 5 open issues. Frequent releases and a near-empty tracker from an engaged single maintainer — strong activity, with single-maintainer concentration as the risk.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the library. Downloaded panoramas remain the imagery providers' copyrighted content.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. The substantive constraints are external: providers' terms of service may prohibit programmatic access, and panorama imagery is copyrighted, so republication in a story needs a rights assessment or fair-dealing judgement.
costs: No fee and no API keys for the internal interfaces — which is precisely why terms-of-service risk substitutes for monetary cost. Negligible compute; storage for panoramas.
privacy: Requests go directly to Google, Apple, Yandex or Mapillary, disclosing the coordinates you are examining. The Yandex case deserves particular thought in hostile-state reporting. Use a dedicated egress.
alternatives: Manual browsing of Street View, Look Around and Yandex Panorama — slower, same disclosure, no terms risk from automation
Mapillary API for openly licensed crowd-sourced imagery
Satellite imagery via sentinelhub-py where street-level is unavailable
blockers: Uses providers' internal interfaces — terms-of-service risk and breakage; queries disclose target coordinates to the providers
summary: Python library for downloading panoramas and metadata from several street-level imagery services, including Google Street View…

name: SuperGlue (pretrained network)
purpose: Graph-neural-network feature matcher that pairs keypoints between two images, widely used to establish whether two photographs show the same place or object from different viewpoints.
journalism_use_case: In principle the strongest available method for confirming a geolocation hypothesis: match keypoints between a photograph and a street-level panorama or satellite image to establish that they show the same building or street from different angles — turning a visual hunch into a demonstrable correspondence.
pros: Technically the reference feature matcher of its generation, widely cited and effective at matching across viewpoint, lighting and season changes
The capability it provides — demonstrable keypoint correspondence between two images — is the most rigorous geolocation confirmation available short of ground truth
Well-documented with reproducible demos, so the method is understandable and the output is visually explainable to an editor
cons: BLOCKER, verified in this session: the LICENSE is a Magic Leap 'SOFTWARE LICENSE AGREEMENT — ACADEMIC OR NON-PROFIT ORGANIZATION NONCOMMERCIAL RESEARCH USE ONLY' agreement between the licensee's academic institution or non-profit and Magic Leap. A commercially operated newsroom cannot use it
Dormant: last push 2024-08-30, no releases, 60 open issues against 4,107 stars — no maintenance and no prospect of a licence change
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION, so automated licence scanning does not flag the restriction — it is easy to adopt this by accident, which is why it is recorded as a lead
Superseded technically as well: newer matchers (LightGlue and successors) are faster and often better, so the restriction costs you less than it would have in 2021
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The decisive documented fact, established in this session by reading the licence blob: the agreement is restricted to academic or non-profit noncommercial research use only (recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md as lead L9). 4,107 stars with 60 open issues and no activity since August 2024.
assessment: Avoid for new deployment in a commercial newsroom — this is a licence conclusion, not a technical one, and it is the most easily missed blocker in the geolocation toolchain because the restriction is invisible to SPDX scanners. Use LoFTR (Apache-2.0) or Hierarchical-Localization (Apache-2.0) instead, while checking that an hloc pipeline you enable does not itself pull SuperGlue weights. If you work with a university partner, they can use it under their own institutional licence.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-08-30, no releases or tags, SPDX NOASSERTION (actual: Magic Leap noncommercial academic agreement), 4,107 stars, 60 open issues. Over two years without activity from a corporate research lab; no indication of further work.
licence: NOT OSS — Magic Leap 'SOFTWARE LICENSE AGREEMENT: ACADEMIC OR NON-PROFIT ORGANIZATION NONCOMMERCIAL RESEARCH USE ONLY' (licence blob read 2026-11-17; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: Same agreement covers the pretrained weights.
licence_restrictions: Commercial use prohibited. The agreement is explicitly between an academic institution or non-profit (or an individual acting as such) and Magic Leap. A commercially operated newsroom has no licence, and NGO status does not automatically qualify — read the agreement before assuming it does.
costs: No fee for permitted academic/non-profit use; no commercial licence path is published. GPU for inference.
privacy: Local inference, so case images stay on your machine — which is of little use given the licence position.
alternatives: LoFTR (Apache-2.0) — recommended permissive alternative for detector-free matching
Hierarchical-Localization / hloc (Apache-2.0) for a full localisation pipeline, but verify which matcher weights you enable
A university partner operating SuperGlue under their own institutional licence
blockers: Noncommercial academic-only licence — unusable by a commercial newsroom, and invisible to SPDX scanners
summary: Graph-neural-network feature matcher that pairs keypoints between two images, widely used to establish whether two photographs…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: LoFTR
purpose: Detector-free local feature matching using transformers, establishing dense correspondences between two images without first detecting keypoints, which works better on low-texture surfaces.
journalism_use_case: The permissively licensed route to confirming a geolocation hypothesis by matching a photograph against a panorama or satellite image. Detector-free matching is particularly useful on the low-texture surfaces common in built environments — plain walls, roads, fields — where keypoint detectors find nothing.
pros: Apache-2.0 for both code and the published weights, which makes it the commercially usable alternative to SuperGlue — the single most important property for your context
Detector-free design handles low-texture scenes better than keypoint-based matchers, which is a real advantage on building façades and open ground
Matching output is visually explainable: you can show an editor the correspondence lines between two images, which is persuasive and checkable
cons: Dormant: last push 2024-05-31, no releases, 95 open issues against 2,981 stars — over two years without maintenance, and the dependency stack of that period will need pinning
Research code rather than a tool: no CLI ergonomics, and integrating it into a repeatable workflow is engineering work
Correspondence quality degrades with large viewpoint or seasonal differences, and a confident-looking match set can still be wrong — it is evidence to be assessed, not proof
GPU effectively required for practical use, and inference on many candidate pairs is slow
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 2,981 stars with 95 open issues, no releases, last push 2024-05-31, Apache-2.0 per the GitHub API. Its standing as a leading detector-free matcher is established in the computer-vision literature; the Apache-2.0 position is the practically decisive fact here.
assessment: The matcher I would use, on licence grounds, despite the dormancy — and the dormancy is tolerable because the weights and method are fixed artefacts rather than a service. For your profile the sensible approach is to containerise it once with pinned dependencies and treat it as a stable internal capability. Present output as a correspondence analysis supporting a geolocation, with the match visualisation published alongside the claim so readers can judge it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-05-31, no releases or tags, 95 open issues, 2,981 stars, Apache-2.0. Over two years without commits. Mitigated by the nature of the artefact: fixed weights plus a research implementation degrade only through dependency rot, which pinning addresses.
model_or_data_licence: Apache-2.0 per the repository; weights published by the authors under the same terms.
licence_restrictions: None identified — the key contrast with SuperGlue. Verify the specific weights file you download, since research repositories occasionally distribute additional checkpoints under different terms.
costs: No fee. GPU needed for practical throughput; weights are a modest download. Engineering time to containerise and integrate is the real cost. Estimate.
privacy: Local inference — case images and reference panoramas stay on your machine, which matters because the alternative (a hosted matching service) would receive both.
alternatives: Hierarchical-Localization (hloc) for a full pipeline, checking which matcher weights it pulls
SuperGlue — avoid: noncommercial licence
Manual visual comparison, which remains the fallback and is what the match analysis supports rather than replaces
blockers: Dormant since mid-2024 — pin dependencies and expect to own maintenance
summary: Detector-free local feature matching using transformers, establishing dense correspondences between two images without first…

name: Hierarchical-Localization (hloc)
maintainer: Computer Vision and Geometry Group, ETH Zurich (cvg)
purpose: Modular visual-localisation toolbox that combines image retrieval, local feature extraction and matching, and structure-from-motion to estimate the camera pose of a query image within a reference reconstruction.
journalism_use_case: The most rigorous available approach to placing a photograph: build a reference reconstruction of a candidate area from panoramas or collected imagery, then localise the query photograph within it, yielding an estimated camera position rather than just a 'same place' judgement.
pros: Produces an estimated camera pose, which is a stronger and more specific result than pairwise matching — you can say where the photographer stood, not merely that the places match
Modular design lets you swap retrieval and matching components, so you can deliberately select Apache-2.0 parts and avoid restricted ones
Apache-2.0 on the framework itself, with substantial community adoption (4,268 stars) and relatively recent activity (pushed 2025-12-10)
Backed by a serious academic group with published methodology, so the technique is citable
cons: Its default and documented pipelines can pull SuperGlue weights, which carry Magic Leap's noncommercial academic licence — so an out-of-the-box hloc run may import a restriction the Apache-2.0 framework licence does not cover. This is the specific trap to avoid
Heavy: structure-from-motion over a reference set is computationally expensive and requires building a reconstruction before you can localise anything
Slowing cadence: last release v1.4 (2023-07-20) and last push 2025-12-10, with 174 open issues — maintained but not briskly
Substantial expertise required; this is the most technically demanding item in this segment and not usable without a computer-vision-literate engineer
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 4,268 stars with 174 open issues, release v1.4 (2023-07-20), last push 2025-12-10, Apache-2.0. The SuperGlue licence interaction is a finding of this session (lead L9): hloc's framework licence is permissive but its component weights are not uniformly so.
assessment: The right tool for a high-stakes geolocation where an estimated camera position would materially strengthen the story — and worth the effort only then. For your profile the mandatory step before use is a component audit: configure hloc with Apache-2.0 matchers (LoFTR or a permissive alternative) and explicitly disable SuperGlue, because the default path imports a noncommercial licence silently. Document the component choices in the methodology note so the result is both reproducible and licence-clean.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-12-10, latest release v1.4 (2023-07-20), 4,268 stars, 174 open issues. Nearly a year since the last push and over three years since a release, but substantial community use and no deprecation. Stable-low rather than declining, with the caveat that an unmaintained CV pipeline accumulates dependency debt.
model_or_data_licence: MIXED AND MATERIAL: the framework is Apache-2.0, but default pipelines can fetch SuperGlue weights under Magic Leap's noncommercial academic agreement. Component weights must be audited individually.
licence_restrictions: The framework imposes nothing, but enabling SuperGlue imports a noncommercial restriction that would bar commercial publication. Select and document permissive components explicitly.
costs: No fee. Significant GPU and compute for reconstruction and localisation; engineer time is the dominant cost. Estimate; assumes self-hosted GPU and an existing reference imagery set.
privacy: Local processing of local imagery. Note that assembling the reference set (downloading many panoramas for a candidate area) discloses that area of interest to the imagery provider.
alternatives: LoFTR alone for pairwise matching without reconstruction — much simpler
Manual geolocation against panoramas, which remains the standard practice
A university partner with existing hloc expertise and an institutional licence covering SuperGlue
blockers: Default pipelines can pull noncommercially licensed SuperGlue weights — component audit required
summary: Modular visual-localisation toolbox that combines image retrieval, local feature extraction and matching…

name: Atlos
purpose: Collaborative workspace for visual investigations: ingests media, tracks per-incident verification status, assigns work, records geolocation and metadata findings, and maintains an auditable history of who concluded what.
journalism_use_case: The missing workflow layer for large-scale visual verification: a team documenting hundreds of incidents in a conflict can track which videos have been geolocated, by whom, with what confidence and what evidence — replacing the spreadsheet that every such project otherwise collapses into.
pros: Solves the organisational problem that defeats large verification projects — tracking status, attribution and evidence across hundreds of incidents — which no other tool in this catalogue addresses
Auditable per-incident history means a published dataset of verified incidents can withstand scrutiny about how each conclusion was reached, which matters enormously for accountability work
GPL-3.0 and self-hostable, so sensitive incident data and contributor identities stay under your control
Purpose-built for human-rights and conflict documentation rather than adapted from generic case management
cons: Small project: 97 stars with 92 open issues and the last release v1.2.17 (2025-09-29) against a 2026-10-23 push — a high backlog ratio and slowing release cadence for infrastructure holding an investigation's core records
Elixir/Phoenix stack is unusual in most newsrooms, so self-hosting requires someone willing to learn it — a real adoption barrier
Hosted option means incident data and contributor activity sit with a third party, which for conflict documentation involving witness-supplied media is a significant decision
Workflow-focused: it organises verification but performs none of it, so it sits on top of the rest of this segment's tooling
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 97 stars with 92 open issues, release v1.2.17 (2025-09-29), last push 2026-10-23, GPL-3.0. Atlos positions itself for conflict and human-rights documentation; I verified no specific deployment, so adoption claims are unestablished here.
assessment: The right answer if you run a project documenting many incidents, and the only serious open option for that workflow — but adopt it with eyes open about project scale. For your profile: pilot it self-hosted if someone can own an Elixir deployment, keep a documented export path so the records are not trapped if the project slows further, and prefer self-hosting over the hosted service wherever witness-supplied media is involved. The alternative is a well-disciplined Datasette-over-SQLite workflow, which is less capable but fully under your control.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-23, latest release v1.2.17 (2025-09-29), 97 stars, 92 open issues. Commits continue but no release in fourteen months and an open-issue count approaching the star count — a small team under strain. Declining rather than dormant, and worth monitoring because the data it would hold is critical.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Media and incident records you store are third-party content with their own rights and, often, serious privacy implications.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0: a modified self-hosted instance offered to users obliges source publication. Internal use unaffected.
costs: No software fee. Self-hosting estimate: an Elixir/Phoenix application plus PostgreSQL and media storage — one moderate VM plus storage growing with media volume, and the dominant cost is the unfamiliar stack's operational learning. Hosted pricing was not verified in this survey. Assumptions: self-hosted, moderate incident volume.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps incident records, media and contributor activity under your control — important because this data can identify witnesses and victims. The hosted option places all of that with a third party, which for conflict documentation is a decision requiring explicit justification.
alternatives: Datasette over a disciplined SQLite schema for a lower-tech but fully controlled equivalent
Uwazi for human-rights documentation with a document rather than incident focus
A shared spreadsheet with strict conventions — what Atlos exists to replace, and what most projects actually use
summary: Collaborative workspace for visual investigations: ingests media, tracks per-incident verification status, assigns work…
